textbook: Clean cutaway textbook illustration of a single infected epithelial host cell showing the Chlamydia felis developmental cycle — the classic teaching plate for this organism. The inclusion is a large round compartment bounded by its own thin, distinct, pale coral inclusion membrane (a different, separate outline from the nucleus's own thin dark envelope line), occupying roughly half the cell's interior, and packed with TWO clearly different round particle types so their size and density contrast is immediately obvious: (1) roughly sixty to eighty tiny ELEMENTARY BODIES (EBs), rendered as small, uniformly solid, deep maroon-burgundy dots — dense, dark, and clustered in tight groups, each about the size of a pinhead relative to the inclusion; and (2) a much smaller number (six to ten) of clearly larger RETICULATE BODIES (RBs), rendered as pale lilac-lavender round bodies with a softer, semi-translucent, lightly mottled interior — each RB's diameter is two to three times an EB's diameter and visibly lighter/less dense, scattered among the EB clusters, some shown mid-division as a gently pinched figure-eight (binary fission). Outside the cell, in the cell-free margin at one corner, show two or three additional free elementary bodies (identical tiny dense maroon dots) approaching and one just touching the outer teal cell membrane, illustrating attachment — these are clearly extracellular and separate from the intracellular inclusion cluster.
